analyst_mode.intro: You filed your report. Below is what your investigation actually did — one OSINT concept at a time. This is not a scorecard. It is a walk-through of the techniques this case relied on and how each one showed up in your evidence.

concepts.title: Attribution ≠ Identification
concepts.why_it_mattered: The photograph is of a real person. That doesn't make the real person the operator of the account. Attribution is about who controls a profile. Identification is about who is in an image. Different questions, different evidence, different sources.

player_observations.text: You examined the account under investigation and separately examined a real person whose photographs matched the account's content.
Your evidence contains two distinct individuals: the person whose photographs the account uses, and a separate person tied to the operator handle.

concepts.real_world_reference: Attribution / image research — reverse-image services such as Google Lens or Yandex Images can surface possible sources for a photograph. A face match remains a lead about who is in the image, not proof of who controls the account.

concepts.title: Content overlap as evidence
concepts.why_it_mattered: When the same images and near-identical captions appear on two different accounts, the overlap itself is data. The direction of the copy is decided by other evidence — timing, ownership, provenance — not by the overlap alone.

player_observations.text: You collected both accounts that carry the same imagery, keeping them alongside each other in your evidence.

concepts.real_world_reference: Content forensics — visual comparison, EXIF inspection and reverse-image lookups are the standard tools for establishing that two posts share source material.

concepts.title: Temporal precedence
concepts.why_it_mattered: If a photograph is documented in a public archive at date A, and another account carrying that same photograph is documented no earlier than date B, and A predates B, then the later account cannot be the origin of the material. Temporal precedence turns a plausible story into a supported one.

player_observations.text: You pulled the earliest indexed capture available for the account under investigation.
You pulled an archived capture that shows the source material existed on the other account before that.

concepts.real_world_reference: Temporal proof — The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine, archive.today and site-specific archives can establish that a page or a post existed at a specific point in time.

concepts.title: Handle-to-identity leak
concepts.why_it_mattered: The same handle can be registered on multiple platforms under different display metadata. When a public-metadata lookup on one platform returns a different real name than the persona presented on another, the mismatch is a lead about the operator — not a conclusion, but a lead worth following.

player_observations.text: You looked up the account's handle on a separate platform and captured the display name that came back with it.
You then searched that display name and captured a second, long-standing handle attached to the same name.

concepts.real_world_reference: Username discovery — tools such as Maigret and Sherlock enumerate reused usernames across public services. A shared handle is a lead; a real name binding two handles is stronger.

concepts.title: Independent corroboration
concepts.why_it_mattered: A subject's own bio is a claim. A record in an unrelated public database — a guild registry, a business directory, a professional certification — is corroboration. The distinction is about the source of the assertion, not about how confident the assertion sounds.

player_observations.text: You obtained a public-record match that corroborates one subject's stated professional location through more than one independent register.
You checked another subject's stated location against public records and captured the result even though nothing corroborated the claim.

concepts.real_world_reference: Independent corroboration — public registries, professional guilds, licensing bodies and organizational directories can independently support (or fail to support) a self-claimed presence. Absence of a record is not proof of a false claim, only absence of corroboration.

hook.text: This case was inspired by real OSINT investigations into identity fabrication on public platforms.
